prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the development of incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, which is unusual, but opening support is not merit, so I restate the scientific case. The arc runs from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36), through receptor biology, to long-acting analogues that are now in use by millions. It has been independently confirmed by large randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. It is original, conceptually clean and mature. Holst (physiology), Drucker (biology and translational concept) and Knudsen (long-acting analogues that made the therapy practical) cover mechanism through drug, and a single prize with a clear citation can recognize that chain.
statement.case_against: The credit is the weakest point. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide is a real contribution, the three-person cap forces an exclusion, and the Habener group is not on the credited list at all. Honoring an industrial drug developer while leaving out a peptide-chemistry pioneer risks an arguable injustice. There is also a risk that the prize reads as a drug-development prize rather than a physiological discovery. I accept that risk because the physiology (Holst, Drucker) is anchored in the same citation.

responses.point: Perlmann would credit Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, arguing that Knudsen's role was largely industrial development and that Mojsov identified and synthesized the active peptide.
responses.response: I take the Mojsov claim seriously and it is the main reason I hold this configuration with some discomfort. But the active-peptide identification, while necessary, was one step. The chain that changed medicine required making the peptide pharmacologically durable, which was Knudsen's contribution (liraglutide, semaglutide). Omitting that step would leave the citation honoring a hormone discovery without the therapy that justifies the prize. If the committee can agree on a different trio I would not block it, but I would not drop Knudsen for Mojsov without a clear argument for why the translational step is less decisive.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks GLP-1 first with Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, calls the Holst and Drucker pairing the defensible core, and treats Knudsen as an industrial developer whose inclusion is questionable. He also gives lower weight to optogenetics and places CAR-T second.
responses.response: I agree that Holst and Drucker are the scientific core and that our disagreement is confined to the third seat. Where I differ is that I do not read industrial status as a reason to exclude. The Nobel criteria concern the discovery and its consequences, not the employer, and the long-acting analogues are what made the physiology matter for patients. I would also add that the optogenetics case is weaker for this prize than for a physics or chemistry one because its medical impact is still early, so I hold it below CAR-T and the UPR.

responses.point: The chair would give the CAR-T prize to June and Sadelain only, treating Rosenberg's adoptive-transfer and early CAR work as adjacent, and flags that Eshhar's early CAR concept complicates priority.
responses.response: I find his two-person trimming of CAR-T more persuasive than my own opening, where I included Rosenberg. Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy is foundational for cellular immunotherapy generally, but the CAR contribution proper is the costimulatory design (Sadelain) and clinical CD19 translation (June). The unresolved Eshhar question is a real obstacle, and it is why I keep CAR-T as an alternative rather than my preferred prize this year.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would also credit Mojsov, and she asks whether an industrial drug-development contribution belongs alongside basic discoveries. She also puts TNF blockade (Feldmann and Maini) and cGAS-STING in her top five.
responses.response: On industrial development, I think the answer is yes when the translation is as inseparable from the discovery as it is here, and Nobel history has honored such steps when the discovery enabled them. I would only be more cautious if the drug had followed obviously from the physiology, which was not the case for the peptide's half-life problem. On TNF, I did not rank it and cannot judge it without seeing the case for it against IL-6 blockade, but I see its maturity, and that would be a stronger candidate than cGAS-STING, whose clinical delivery is still absent.

uncertainties: How to allocate the third seat between Knudsen and Mojsov, and whether the Habener group's early proglucagon work changes that.
Whether the committee prefers a physiology-anchored citation or one anchored on therapy; the wording of the citation could affect who is credited.
Whether Eshhar's early chimeric-receptor concept makes CAR-T attribution unworkable with the credited names, which determines whether B039 is a viable alternative this year.
Long-term safety and durability of effects of incretin therapy are still being characterized.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My recorded co-authorship of the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper and my work with several KI colleagues concern single-cell and spatial methods that are not among the shortlisted ballots, and I did not infer any tie from shared institutions or topics.
